programs.name: HUSKY Health (Medicaid for seniors/disabled)
programs.tagline: Comprehensive health coverage including long-term care for Connecticut seniors with limited income and assets

localEntities.name: Department of Social Services (DSS) statewide; local DSS offices for in-person

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 65+ or disabled and lives in Connecticut, HUSKY Health C (Medicaid) can cover all their medical care plus long-term services to help them stay at home. This includes doctor visits, prescriptions, dental, vision, and crucially for aging loved ones, home care, adult day programs, and nursing home care if needed.

The program has different income limits depending on what services your loved one needs. Standard coverage requires income under $851/month for a single person, but if your loved one needs home care or nursing home care, they can qualify with income up to $2,982/month. Asset limits also apply: $1,600 for a single person in most cases.

Because HUSKY Health C is comprehensive Medicaid, your loved one won't pay premiums, deductibles, or copays for covered services. One program manages all their health care instead of coordinating between Medicare and separate providers.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep their house if it's worth more than the asset limit?
faqs.answer: Yes, your loved one's primary home is generally exempt from the asset limit as long as they live in it or intend to return. There may be equity limits for Long-Term Services & Supports, but the home itself doesn't count toward the $1,600 limit.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's income is slightly over the limit?
faqs.answer: Your loved one may still qualify through a spend-down process, where they pay their excess income toward medical bills each month. The exact amount depends on how much they're over the limit. Call DSS on 1-855-626-6632 to discuss spend-down options.

faqs.question: Can I apply for HUSKY Health C and Medicare Savings Programs at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you should. If your loved one qualifies for HUSKY Health C, they automatically qualify for Medicare Savings Programs, which will cover their Medicare premiums and potentially deductibles and copays. Apply for both through the same application.

faqs.question: How long does the level of care assessment take for long-term services?
faqs.answer: The clinical assessment typically takes 2-4 weeks to schedule and complete. An assessor will evaluate your loved one's ability to perform daily activities like bathing, dressing, and medication management. This determines whether they qualify for home care services or nursing home coverage.

faqs.question: What if my loved one has assets in another state?
faqs.answer: All assets count toward the limit regardless of location, including out-of-state bank accounts, property, or investments. You'll need to provide documentation for all assets during the application process, including the 5-year lookback for Long-Term Services & Supports.

faqs.question: Can my loved one choose their own home care provider under HUSKY Health C?
faqs.answer: Yes, Connecticut allows consumer-directed care where your loved one can hire their own home care workers, including family members in some cases. This gives more flexibility than agency-provided care, but requires managing payroll and training responsibilities.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's condition changes after enrollment?
faqs.answer: HUSKY Health C coverage adjusts as your loved one's needs change. If they need more care, contact their managed care organization to request a reassessment. If their health improves significantly, they may be moved to a different coverage level during annual reviews.

faqs.question: Will applying for Long-Term Services & Supports affect my inheritance?
faqs.answer: Connecticut may seek estate recovery after your loved one's death to recoup long-term care costs, but this typically only applies to assets that go through probate. The primary home is often protected if a surviving spouse or disabled child lives there. Consult an elder law attorney about asset protection strategies.

programs.name: Connecticut Home Care Program for Elders (CHCPE) - Medicare Savings
programs.tagline: Home care services to keep your loved one out of a nursing home, plus Medicare premium savings.

localEntities.name: Western CT Area Agency on Aging (WCAAA)
Department of Social Services (DSS) regional offices

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 65+ and needs help with bathing, dressing, or medication management, CHCPE provides home care services to avoid nursing home placement. The program covers up to 70 hours per week of in-home assistance with daily activities, depending on your loved one's functional needs and income level.

Because CHCPE includes Medicare Savings Program benefits, qualified participants also get their Medicare Part B premiums covered ($185/month in 2026) plus deductibles and co-insurance. State-funded participants pay only 3% of service costs, while Medicaid-funded services have no client cost-share.

The program has two tracks: Medicaid-funded (income limit $1,956/month for singles in 2025) and state-funded (no income limit but asset limits apply). All participants must demonstrate risk of nursing home placement by needing assistance with at least one activity of daily living.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep their house if it's worth more than the asset limit?
faqs.answer: Yes, the primary home is typically exempt from asset limits regardless of value. However, for Medicaid-funded services, the state may place a lien on the home for estate recovery after death. Medicare Savings Program benefits have no asset limits at all.

faqs.question: What's the difference between state-funded and Medicaid-funded CHCPE?
faqs.answer: State-funded has no income limit but your loved one pays 3% of service costs and faces asset limits. Medicaid-funded has income limits ($1,956/month for singles) but no client cost-share, and includes a 5-year lookback for asset transfers.

faqs.question: How long is the waitlist really?
faqs.answer: State-funded services may start quickly with no waitlist. Medicaid waiver funding can have 2+ year waits depending on your region and your loved one's priority level. Higher functional needs get priority placement.

faqs.question: Can I apply for my loved one if they have dementia?
faqs.answer: Yes, adult children can apply on behalf of parents with cognitive impairment. You'll need to provide power of attorney documents or become their legal representative through the probate court process.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income is too high for Medicaid-funded services?
faqs.answer: They can still qualify for state-funded CHCPE services with no income limit, though they'll pay 3% of service costs. They may also qualify for Medicare Savings Program benefits which have higher income limits ($2,807/month for QMB in 2026).

faqs.question: Can my loved one get both CHCPE and Medicare Savings Program benefits?
faqs.answer: Yes, these programs are often bundled together. Medicare Savings covers Part B premiums, deductibles and co-insurance, while CHCPE provides the actual home care services. The eligibility requirements and asset rules differ between the two components.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's needs increase after enrollment?
faqs.answer: Services can be adjusted up to 70 hours per week based on reassessments. Your loved one's care coordinator will evaluate changing needs and modify the service plan accordingly. Priority levels may also change based on functional decline.

faqs.question: Will the state try to recover money from my loved one's estate?
faqs.answer: For Medicaid-funded CHCPE services, Connecticut may seek estate recovery after death. However, Medicare Savings Program benefits have no estate recovery. State-funded services have different recovery rules, check with your caseworker about specific policies.

programs.name: SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program)
programs.tagline: Up to $298 per month for groceries if your loved one is on a fixed income

localEntities.name: Local DSS offices; find via portal.ct.gov/dss

programs.intro:
If your loved one is struggling to afford groceries on Social Security or a pension, SNAP provides monthly benefits loaded onto an EBT card for food purchases. A single person can receive up to $298 per month, while a two-person household can get up to $546 monthly, the exact amount depends on income after deductions like medical expenses and housing costs.

Connecticut makes SNAP easier for seniors by allowing households with someone 60 or older to skip the strict gross income test and offering a simplified application. Your loved one can use SNAP benefits at grocery stores for food items (not prepared meals, alcohol, or tobacco), making their Social Security check stretch further each month.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep SNAP if they also get Medicaid?
faqs.answer: Yes, your loved one can receive both SNAP and Medicaid at the same time. Having one benefit doesn't disqualify them from the other, and the application processes are separate.

faqs.question: What if my loved one lives with me but we buy groceries separately?
faqs.answer: If your loved one buys and prepares food separately from your household, they can apply as a one-person household even if living in your home. The key is whether they shop and cook independently.

faqs.question: Can I apply for SNAP on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can apply as an authorized representative if your loved one gives written permission or if you have power of attorney. You can complete the application and attend interviews on their behalf.

faqs.question: Will my loved one's home or car count against the asset limit?
faqs.answer: No, the primary home and vehicles are exempt from SNAP asset limits. Only countable assets like bank accounts and stocks matter, and most Connecticut applicants face no asset limit anyway.

faqs.question: How much will my loved one actually receive each month?
faqs.answer: SNAP calculates benefits as the maximum allotment minus 30% of net income. For example, a single person with $1,000 net monthly income would receive $298 (max) minus $300 (30% of income), so they'd get the minimum benefit amount.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's income changes after approval?
faqs.answer: Report income changes within 10 days to your local DSS office. Benefits will be recalculated, and your loved one may need to complete a review every 12 months to continue receiving SNAP.

faqs.question: Can SNAP benefits be used for groceries delivered to the home?
faqs.answer: Yes, many grocery stores that accept EBT now offer delivery and pickup services. Your loved one can use their EBT card for online grocery orders from participating retailers like Amazon and Walmart.

faqs.question: What if the DSS office says my loved one makes too much money?
faqs.answer: Ask specifically about the elderly rules, households with someone 60+ can skip the gross income test and may qualify based on net income after deductions. High medical or housing costs can significantly reduce countable income.

programs.name: Connecticut Energy Assistance Program (CEAP)
programs.tagline: Help your loved one get $295-$645 toward heating bills this winter, with emergency assistance available for fuel crises.

localEntities.name: Regional providers like New Opportunities Inc., Alliance for Community Empowerment

programs.intro:
If your loved one struggles with heating bills in Connecticut, CEAP can provide $295-$645 toward their energy costs this winter. Because the program pays utility companies directly, your loved one won't handle cash, the assistance goes straight toward their heating bill, electric bill, or fuel delivery. Households with elderly members, disabled individuals, or children under 6 receive higher benefit amounts.

The program runs from September 1, 2025 through May 29, 2026, but funds are limited and distributed first-come, first-served. Because crisis assistance is available for households facing fuel emergencies, eligible families can get fuel delivery authorization within 18 hours if they're running out of heating oil or propane.

Income limit: $47,764/year for a single person, $62,460 for a couple (2025-2026). No asset test this year. If your loved one receives SNAP, SSI, or TANF, they automatically qualify regardless of other income.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply if they're behind on their electric bill?
faqs.answer: Yes. CEAP can help with past-due balances and may provide shut-off protection. The program can also set up payment plans and help with equipment repair or replacement. Include any shut-off notices when applying.

faqs.question: What if my loved one rents and heat is included in their rent?
faqs.answer: Your loved one can still get help through the rental assistance portion of CEAP, which provides $75-$125 toward rent. You'll need to provide a rent receipt or lease agreement showing heat is included.

faqs.question: How much more do vulnerable households actually get?
faqs.answer: Vulnerable households (with elderly, disabled, or children under 6) receive $345-$645 instead of the standard $295-$595. That's an extra $50 in assistance. Make sure to indicate vulnerable status when applying.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get crisis help if they run out of heating oil?
faqs.answer: Yes, but only if they use deliverable fuels like oil or propane, and only after their basic CEAP benefit is used up. Crisis benefits provide $425 per occurrence, up to 3 times per season, with fuel delivery authorization within 18 hours.

faqs.question: What if my loved one gets Social Security but can't find their award letter?
faqs.answer: Connecticut DSS cannot verify Social Security benefits directly, so the award letter is required. Your loved one can get a replacement letter by calling Social Security at (800) 772-1213 or logging into their my Social Security account online.

faqs.question: Is it too late to apply if the heating season already started?
faqs.answer: No. The application window runs from September 1, 2025 through May 29, 2026. However, funds are limited and distributed first-come, first-served, so applying earlier in the season increases chances of receiving assistance.

faqs.question: Can I apply for my loved one if they can't do it themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can apply on behalf of elderly loved ones. You'll need to provide all the same documentation and may need to show you have permission to act on their behalf. Contact your regional provider to discuss the specific process.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one moves to a different town in Connecticut during the heating season?
faqs.answer: Your loved one should contact their new regional provider immediately. Since CEAP is administered by different agencies across Connecticut, they may need to transfer their case or reapply through the new service area.

programs.name: Weatherization Assistance Program
programs.tagline: Free home energy improvements worth up to $15,000 to reduce your loved one's heating and cooling bills

localEntities.name: Statewide CAA network, local non-profits (e.g., CRT, PSH); find via 2-1-1 or DEEP email

programs.intro:
If your loved one's home in Connecticut is drafty, poorly insulated, or expensive to heat and cool, they may qualify for free weatherization services worth up to $15,000. The Weatherization Assistance Program provides energy audits, insulation, air sealing, heating system tune-ups, and safety repairs at no cost to income-eligible households.

Priority goes to households with seniors 60+, people with disabilities, or those spending 6% or more of their income on energy bills. Because the program covers both energy improvements ($10,000 maximum) and health/safety repairs ($2,500 maximum), your loved one's home becomes more comfortable while reducing monthly utility costs.

The program requires joint application with Connecticut's Energy Assistance Program through 2-1-1. Your loved one's home cannot have been weatherized by any federal program in the past 15 years, and cannot be listed for sale or in foreclosure proceedings.

otherRequirements: Home not weatherized by WAP, LIHEAP, HUD, or USDA in past 15 years
Home not for sale or in foreclosure proceedings
For multi-family properties: at least 2/3 of tenants must be income-eligible

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply for weatherization if they're a renter?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the landlord may need to contribute 20% of material costs, up to $500 per unit. For multi-family properties, at least two-thirds of tenants must be income-eligible. The landlord must also agree not to sell the property for 6 months after work completion.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's home was weatherized years ago through a utility program?
faqs.answer: Your loved one can still qualify as long as the previous weatherization wasn't done by WAP, LIHEAP, HUD, or USDA programs within the past 15 years. Utility company programs like Energize Connecticut don't disqualify them.

faqs.question: How much priority do seniors actually get in the waitlist?
faqs.answer: Households with seniors 60+, people with disabilities, or those spending 6% or more of income on energy get priority scheduling. While exact wait times aren't published, priority households typically get scheduled for energy audits within a few months rather than facing longer delays.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, adult children can help with the application process. Call 2-1-1 and explain you're applying for your loved one. You'll need to bring your loved one's income documentation and home ownership proof to the intake appointment.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's house needs more than $15,000 in work?
faqs.answer: The program caps at $10,000 for energy measures, $2,500 for health/safety repairs, and $2,500 for incidental repairs ($15,000 total for single-family homes). Work exceeding these limits requires special review and approval, which isn't guaranteed.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get both Energy Assistance and Weatherization in the same year?
faqs.answer: Yes, they use the same application through 2-1-1. Energy Assistance helps with current utility bills while Weatherization provides long-term home improvements. Both programs complement each other and share the same income eligibility requirements.

programs.name: CHOICES (CT SHIP)
programs.tagline: Free Medicare counseling to help your loved one navigate plans, save money, and avoid enrollment mistakes.
programs.intro:
If your loved one is approaching Medicare eligibility or struggling to understand their current coverage, CHOICES provides free one-on-one counseling to help them make informed decisions. This is Connecticut's version of the federal SHIP program (State Health Insurance Assistance Program), offering unbiased guidance on Medicare Parts A, B, C, and D, plus help finding cost-assistance programs like the Medicare Savings Program and Low-Income Subsidy.

Because CHOICES counselors are trained volunteers with no financial stake in insurance sales, your loved one gets honest advice tailored to their specific needs and budget. The service is available to all Medicare-eligible Connecticut residents regardless of income, plus their family caregivers and anyone preparing for Medicare enrollment.

Counselors can help compare Medicare Advantage plans during Open Enrollment (October 15 - December 7), screen for programs that could lower prescription costs, and resolve claims disputes. Call 800-994-9422 to connect with a local counselor.

otherRequirements: Must be Medicare-eligible: US citizens or permanent residents aged 65+, or younger people with disabilities who have collected SSDI for 24 months, or those with 40 quarters of Social Security/Railroad Retirement work history
Connecticut residency required

applicationGuide.summary: Call 800-994-9422 to connect with a local counselor, no formal application needed, counseling provided immediately upon contact.

steps.description: Call 800-994-9422 to be connected to a local SHIP counselor in your area.

steps.description: The counselor will arrange a convenient time for one-on-one guidance, either by phone or at an accessible location near you.

steps.title: Prepare your Medicare information

applicationGuide.processingTime: Counseling provided upon contact, no processing time required
applicationGuide.tip: Call during Open Enrollment (October 15 - December 7) as early as possible, as counselors get busiest closer to the December 7 deadline.

faqs.question: Can I get help for my loved one even if they're already enrolled in Medicare?
faqs.answer: Yes. CHOICES counselors help with ongoing Medicare questions, plan comparisons during Open Enrollment, prescription drug coverage issues, and claims disputes. They can also screen your loved one for cost-assistance programs they may not know about, like the Medicare Savings Program that could eliminate their Part B premium.

faqs.question: Is this really free, or will they try to sell us insurance?
faqs.answer: Completely free with no sales pressure. CHOICES counselors are trained volunteers who don't sell insurance or receive commissions. Their only goal is to help you understand Medicare options and find the most cost-effective coverage for your loved one's specific health needs and budget.

faqs.question: What's the difference between calling CHOICES versus talking to an insurance agent?
faqs.answer: Insurance agents can only sell plans from their company and earn commissions on what they sell. CHOICES counselors can compare all available Medicare options in Connecticut, including Original Medicare, all Medicare Advantage plans, and all Part D prescription plans, with no financial bias toward any particular insurer.

programs.name: Connecticut Statewide Respite Care Program
programs.tagline: Up to $7,500 annually to help pay for respite care when your loved one has dementia

localEntities.name: Multiple Area Agencies on Aging throughout Connecticut
Program is partnership between Alzheimer's Association Connecticut Chapter, Area Agencies on Aging, and Connecticut Aging and Disability Services, Bureau of Aging

programs.intro:
If your loved one has Alzheimer's disease or related dementia, Connecticut provides up to $7,500 annually to help pay for respite care services. This program covers adult day care, home health aides, personal care assistants, short-term nursing home stays, and other services that give you breaks from caregiving.

Your loved one must have a physician-confirmed diagnosis of irreversible dementia and annual income below $58,772. Because this is a subsidy program, you'll pay 20% of the service costs (unless waived for financial hardship), and the state covers the rest up to the annual cap. Both you and your loved one must live in Connecticut, and your loved one cannot already receive services through the Connecticut Homecare Program for Elders.
programs.savingsSource: CT ADS: up to $7,500 per year depending on funding and need, minus a 20% co-payment in most cases

structuredEligibility.functionalRequirement: Must have physician-confirmed diagnosis of irreversible and deteriorating dementia (Alzheimer's disease, multi-infarct dementia, Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia, Huntington's disease, normal pressure hydrocephalus, or Pick's disease)

Cannot receive Connecticut Homecare Program for Elders services
Caregiver must be experiencing physical or mental impairments or have primary responsibility for care

faqs.question: Can my loved one get this program if they already receive the Connecticut Homecare Program for Elders?
faqs.answer: No, your loved one cannot receive both programs simultaneously. You'll need to choose which program better fits your loved one's needs. The Homecare Program provides broader services while this respite program focuses specifically on caregiver relief for dementia patients.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income is right at the limit, which number is correct, $58,772 or $48,266?
faqs.answer: The sources show conflicting income limits, suggesting possible updates or regional variations. Call 1-800-994-9422 to verify the current income threshold for your area before applying.

faqs.question: Does the $7,500 annual limit cover the full cost of services?
faqs.answer: No, this is a subsidy program. You'll pay 20% of service costs out-of-pocket, and the state covers the rest up to $7,500 annually. If costs exceed the annual limit, you're responsible for anything above that amount.

faqs.question: Can the 20% co-payment be waived if we can't afford it?
faqs.answer: Yes, the Area Agency on Aging Care Manager can waive the 20% co-payment due to financial hardship. Discuss your financial situation during the assessment process.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's doctor won't fill out the Physician Statement form?
faqs.answer: The physician statement is required and must be completed by a doctor, generic medical records won't substitute. If your current doctor won't complete it, you may need to see a specialist familiar with dementia diagnoses.

faqs.question: Is approval guaranteed if we meet all the eligibility requirements?
faqs.answer: No, the program depends on available state funding. Meeting eligibility requirements puts you in line for services, but approval isn't guaranteed even if you qualify.

faqs.question: Can I hire my own family member as a caregiver through this program?
faqs.answer: The program offers self-directed options where you can hire private caregivers through a fiduciary, but specific rules about hiring family members aren't detailed in available regulations. Ask your Care Manager about family hiring restrictions.

faqs.question: How long does it typically take to get approved and start receiving services?
faqs.answer: Processing timelines aren't specified in available documentation. Call your Area Agency on Aging at 1-800-994-9422 to understand current wait times and processing expectations in your region.

programs.name: Senior Community Service Employment Program (SCSEP)
programs.tagline: Paid job training for unemployed adults 55+, earn minimum wage while learning skills at nonprofits and public agencies

localEntities.name: Associates for Training and Development (A4TD), primary Connecticut provider, Stamford, CT 06831

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 55+ and unemployed, SCSEP provides paid on-the-job training at nonprofits and public agencies. Your loved one earns minimum wage for an average of 20 hours per week while gaining work experience at places like schools, hospitals, senior centers, and day-care centers.

Because this is federally funded job training, your loved one receives career assessment, job placement assistance, and specialized skill training at no cost. The goal is to transition participants into permanent, unsubsidized employment after completing the training program. Career tracks include home health aide, food service, customer service, office administration, stock clerk, and retail sales.

Income must not exceed 125% of the federal poverty level, and priority goes to veterans, those over 65, and people with disabilities or other barriers to employment.

otherRequirements: Must be currently unemployed
Priority enrollment for veterans and qualified spouses of veterans
Priority for individuals over age 65
Priority for individuals with disabilities
Priority for individuals with low literacy skills or limited English proficiency
Priority for rural residents
Priority for homeless or at-risk individuals

steps.title: Await placement match

applicationGuide.tip: Veterans and those over 65 get priority enrollment, mention this status when calling if it applies to your loved one.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply for SCSEP while receiving unemployment benefits?
faqs.answer: No, participants must be unemployed to qualify, which typically means not receiving unemployment compensation. Contact Associates for Training and Development at 203-461-2154 to clarify how unemployment benefits affect eligibility in your loved one's specific situation.

faqs.question: Is this permanent employment or temporary training?
faqs.answer: SCSEP is temporary job training designed as a bridge to permanent employment. Participants work an average of 20 hours per week at minimum wage while receiving career services and job placement assistance. The goal is to transition into unsubsidized employment after completing the training program.

faqs.question: What if my loved one is under 65 and not a veteran, will they still get accepted?
faqs.answer: Yes, but they may face longer wait times. Priority goes first to veterans and qualified spouses, then to those over 65, then to people with disabilities or other barriers to employment. Non-priority applicants are still eligible but may need to wait for available training slots.

programs.name: Long Term Care Ombudsman Program
programs.tagline: Free advocacy when your loved one has problems with their nursing home or assisted living facility.

localEntities.name: Central office: 55 Farmington Avenue, Hartford, CT 06105-3730.
Regional Ombudsman programs (search Community Resources Database for local providers).

programs.intro:
If your loved one lives in a Connecticut nursing home, assisted living, or residential care facility and has problems with care, billing, or treatment, the Long Term Care Ombudsman provides free advocacy. Ombudsmen investigate complaints confidentially, help resolve disputes between residents and facilities, and ensure your loved one's rights are protected.

The program serves residents of all licensed long-term care facilities statewide, regardless of income. Because ombudsmen are independent advocates (not employed by facilities), they can address issues like inadequate care, medication errors, billing disputes, or restrictions on visitors without conflict of interest.

Families considering facility placement can also get information about quality ratings and resident rights before choosing where their loved one will live.

summary: Resident of CT nursing home, assisted living, or residential care facility

faqs.question: Can I call the ombudsman if my loved one hasn't given permission?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can call to discuss concerns and get information. However, the ombudsman cannot act on complaints or investigate without your loved one's permission (unless your loved one lacks capacity and you have legal authority). The ombudsman will keep your call confidential while helping you understand options.

faqs.question: What if the facility retaliates against my loved one for filing a complaint?
faqs.answer: Retaliation is illegal and ombudsmen are trained to prevent it. They work confidentially when possible and can advocate for your loved one's protection. If retaliation occurs, contact the ombudsman immediately at 860-424-5200, they will investigate and can involve state regulators if needed.

faqs.question: Can the ombudsman help before my loved one moves into a facility?
faqs.answer: Yes, families considering placement can get information about facility quality ratings, resident rights, and what questions to ask during visits. Call 860-424-5200 to speak with an ombudsman about choosing the right facility for your loved one's needs.

stateOverview.intro: Connecticut offers 10 major programs to help your aging loved one, from $298/month for groceries to $15,000 in free home energy improvements. Seven of these provide direct financial benefits or services (requiring income/asset limits), while three offer free resources available to any Connecticut senior regardless of income. Most programs target seniors with monthly incomes below $2,152-$2,901, but some like Medicare counseling and ombudsman services help everyone. Start by checking the highest-value programs first: HUSKY Health for comprehensive medical coverage, Connecticut Home Care Program to keep your loved one out of nursing homes, and SNAP for immediate grocery assistance.
